title: The Basics
body:
All roads lead to the City. It is a land rich with trade and culture, a land of ancient dignity. The fay and underfolk both claim that the City predated the coming of humans, but the City is now undeniably the seat of humankind. For generations, men and women of famous heritage and noble blood have ruled the City through ages of feast and ages of famine.

And then, the Underworld opened beneath it.

Beneath the world’s largest metropolis, passages in plaster mines were discovered that led to a gargantuan castle, surrounded by a ruined city, deep inside the stygian depths.

title: The Four Phases
body:
Each adventurer has a personal quest that compels them into the lightless depths. Once their quest is fulfilled, they can finally retire and rest. Until then, it is a cycle of descending into the Underworld and returning to the City to restock and rest.

The flow of the game consists of four distinct phases, each with its own style of play and rules.

### Against canon

Throughout this book, there are references to an implied setting that are never elaborated on. We name and discuss people, places, and historical events without describing them in great detail. This is intentional.

Instead of providing a gazetteer with everything carefully plotted out and a hundred-and-one nonsense fantasy words for you to memorize, we’ve painted with a fairly broad brush. It’s our intention to give you a sense of scope and flavor without bogging the game down with lore to memorize or binding your story to a metaplot. The game world and the storyline are intended to vary from table to table.

It’s our hope that the implied setting of *His Majesty the Worm* stimulates your imagination and allows you to tell the stories that you want to tell.

As the setting details provided invoke a certain aesthetic for you, we hope that you will use them. As the setting details provided feel frustrating in their obscurity or contradictions, we hope you will change them, ignore them, or tear them physically from the book. At times, the provided material will be inherently contradictory, obliging you to make a decision about which version you want to be “true.”

title: The Crawl Phase
body: During the Crawl Phase, the guild explores an interconnected network of dungeons called the Underworld. During this phase, adventurers test their wits and skills against inhospitable forces in order to fulfill their quests. During the Crawl, players charge their Bonds with their guild-mates. The Crawl is where you’ll spend most of your time.

title: The Challenge Phase
body:
A Challenge Phase occurs when you need to focus on the beat-by-beat action. This phase is when choices and consequences bear the hideous, overripe fruit of rotting bodies and terminated possibilities! During a Challenge, play moves from a freeform style to a tactical system. Play is split up into rounds and turns, during which people perform various specific actions.

*“Many sink down and few return to the sunlit lands.”* *– The Silver Chair, C.S. Lewis*

### The Camp Phase

As the adventurers get worn down by journeys and battles, they’ll pause and use the Camp Phase. The focus of the Camp Phase is interpersonal roleplaying, drama, and connections between members of the guild. During this phase, players burn charged Bonds to rest and recover.

### The City Phase

Each delve is punctuated by the City Phase. The City Phase resolves the entire sequence and gives the guild a chance to spend their hard-earned loot, advance their long-term agendas, and reflect on their progress.

### The Four Phases (diagram, p.15)

**City** — Turn in and take new contracts; spend wealth to restock and heal; pursue long-term schemes. 1. Death and Taxes 2. Noteworthy Deeds 3. City Events 4. Turn in Contracts 5. Upkeep 6. City Actions 7. Plan the Next Crawl 8. Restock the Underworld

**Crawl** — Pursue your quest; accumulate wealth and avoid hazards; charge Bonds through roleplaying and fulfilling conditions. 1. Declare you enter the quest 2. A watch passes when you travel to the next room 3. The GM draws on the Meatgrinder table each watch

**Challenge** — Fight the denizens of the Underworld; notch armor; gain Wounds. 1. Set the Scene 2. Draw Challenge Cards 3. Play Initiative 4. Take Turns 5. Minor Actions6 6. End the Round

**Camp** — Burn charged Bonds; heal Wounds; gain Resolve. 1. Camp Actions 2. Break Bread 3. No Rest for the Wicked 4. Recovery 5. End Camp Phase

title: The Flow of the Play
body: Games usually take place at a regularly scheduled time and place. Finding time to play games with other busy people can be challenging. Consistent play is crucial to keeping a game alive. Most sessions have a basic flow:

title: Before play
body:
At the start of a game session, a few important pieces of bookkeeping are taken care of:

### Recap

One player—with help from others at the table, and with corrections from the GM as needed—recaps what happened during the last session. This gets everybody back into the game and refreshes their memory about where they were and what they’re doing.

If this player does an exceptionally good job, the GM may give them a point of Resolve. They may keep this Resolve or give it to another player who needs it.

### Returning players

If anyone misses a session during the Crawl Phase, their adventurer is assumed to be about one room away, trailing behind the main guild. They have been slowed down performing a Camp Action. When the player returns, they tell the table what activity they performed, receive the benefit from it, and rejoin the main group. Some actions (e.g., Fellowship, Train) logically require another adventurer to be “absent” with the returning player; only choose activities that make sense for the circumstances.

*“Pataphysics means ‘beyond metaphysics’; It is the science of imaginary solutions that studies the exceptions rather than laws and aspires to provide imaginary solutions to practical problems.”*

*– Italo Calvino*

title: During play
body:
A typical game session flows between the different phases. Over the course of many game sessions, play will follow this sequence:

- Decide to pursue one adventurer’s quest.
- Adventure through the Underworld (Crawl Phase).
- Struggle against the strange denizens of the Underworld (Challenge Phase).
- Rest as well as possible in the lightless depths (Camp Phase).
- Return to the City, broken and bleeding (City Phase).
- Spend accumulated wealth to heal, stock up on equipment, and pursue long-term projects in the City.
- Pick up a contract to finance the next crawl.
- Descend back into the Underworld in continued pursuit of the current quest while working on their contract (Crawl Phase).
- Repeat.

title: End of play
body:
Play can end after any phase or simply at a specified time. It’s best for the GM to close play when there’s a good stopping point—when one scene has just ended, or just after introducing a new scene (so the players have something to look forward to next week).

The GM can take time at the end of play to get feedback about what the players want to do or where they want to go next. Reminders about when they’ll play next, who might be absent, etc., can be dealt with at this time.

title: Adjudicating the game: GM responses
body:
An RPG is a conversation between the GM and the players. The GM describes a scene and the players describe their actions inside the scene. The GM and the players ask questions of each other to further define their shared textual reality.

The GM adjudicates how the adventurers’ actions impact the world. To this end, GMs are armed with the following four stock phrases:

- “Yes, you can do that.”
- “Say more about what you’re doing.”
- “Draw to see if you can do that.”
- “No, you can’t do that.”

These phrases (and their variants) are the four basic responses that a GM has for answering a player when they ask, “Can my character do…?”

### “Yes, you can do that”

The player describes their adventurer’s actions and the GM simply describes what happens. If there’s nothing preventing the adventurer from succeeding, they simply succeed.

- “It doesn’t seem that the door is locked. You open the door slowly and carefully.”
- “Sure, you can climb the tree. There're plenty of handholds.”
- “You know that it will take a few minutes of hard work and it'll make a shit ton of noise, but of course you can use your felling axe to hack down the wooden door.”

Players portray members of the unfortunate caste called “adventurers.” As such, they have the skills and abilities that you’d assume adventurers would have by default.

In practice, this means you ignore all the uninteresting parts of adventuring. You never test fate to see if an adventurer knows how to kindle a bonfire—they’re competent travelers. Don’t worry about what weapons an adventurer is proficient in—they’re competent fighters.

Even difficult tasks can be resolved without a test of fate as long as: 1. there’s no interesting risk; 2. the adventurer has plenty of time; 3. they have the appropriate tools.

If one of these factors is missing, it’s time to move to one of the other responses.

If an adventurer's actions would incur some sort of penalty, the GM should make that clear and give them a choice.

- If an adventurer’s actions would take a long time to complete, the GM should make this clear. If the player elects to spend the time, the GM draws on the Meatgrinder table to represent time passing; similar to the Moving carefully rules. Draw from the major arcana—torches gutter on a result of I-V.
- If an adventurer's actions would create a lot of noise, the GM should give that info. If the player elects to risk the noise, the GM draws on the Meatgrinder table to represent an interested predator investigating the disturbance; similar to the Loud noises rules. The GM draws from the major arcana—a random encounter occurs on a result of XV-XX.

### “Say more about what you’re doing”

Sometimes it’s not exactly clear what actions the players are describing or what their intentions are. In these cases, the GM should ask for clarification.

- “How exactly are you searching for traps?”

“OK, because of the Linguist talent, you definitely speak the myconid language, but you know that their language is expressed entirely in the medium of spore bursts. How do you intend to communicate with the fungoid?”

- “How can you read the text if you don't have any light?”

Sometimes there is a miscommunication in what the GM has described—the GM might be picturing one thing but the players have understood something very differently. Sometimes there's ambiguity in what the player is trying to do. Asking for clarification keeps the shared hallucination of the game consistent by syncing information between the GM and the player.

The GM can also ask clarifying questions about the tactics that the character would be employing. A player’s statement that they want to “Perform a coup de grace on the vampire” might be more successful depending on the precise methods employed—the GM may want to know what weapons are used, what exactly is done, etc.

Once the GM has achieved clarity with “Say more,” they can then shift to one of the other three basic responses.

### “Draw to see if you can do that”

When an action is fraught with danger or its outcome is uncertain, it’s time to test fate. For an overview of tests of fate.

Tests of fate should be relatively rare and relatively tense. Don’t call for tests of fate for inconsequential actions— only when something of importance hangs in the balance.

- “The door is locked. If you have lockpicks, you can test Pentacles to try and pick the lock.”

### “No, you can’t do that”

Sometimes, actions are not possible or will automatically fail based on the logic of the narrative world.

- “No, you can't really try and tame a dangerous wild beast with a single test of fate. Something like that would need to be done by breaking it over the course of several weeks. You can try and capture it, though, if you want...”
- “No, if you don't have any tools, you don't have any way to pick the lock. There's not any, like, bits of wire just lying around your jail cell.”

### The Challenge Phase

It's worth noting that the rules of the Challenge Phase are more bounded than the freeform nature of standard play. The Challenge Actions and the player's hand of cards usually determine what an adventurer can and can't do. The GM still adjudicates what the players try to do when there's ambiguity:

*"Oh, you're trying to squeeze past the slime as they squelch down the hall? Well, there's not really space to Avoid it — it takes up the entire corridor. Do you want to do something else instead?"*

title: The Major and Minor Arcana
body:
A single **tarot** deck is used in *His Majesty the Worm* to create random results. A tarot deck in its entirety consists of seventy-eight cards of two types: **major arcana** and **minor arcana**. **The GM uses the major arcana cards *except* the Fool.** The major arcarna are numbered and have evocative names like Magician [I] and Wheel of Fortune [X]. Therefore, the GM’s deck has 21 cards, numbered I–XXI.

**Players use the minor arcana cards *plus* the Fool,** which is borrowed from the major arcana deck. There are fifty-six minor arcana cards—reminiscent of a more traditional deck of poker cards—with four suits of fourteen cards. The four suits are Swords, Pentacles, Cups, and Wands. The minor arcana are numbered I–X, and each suit has four face cards.

Each card in the minor arcana has a value. A card’s value equals the number shown on the card. The Fool has the value of 0. Aces have a value of 1. The face cards have the following numeric values:

- Page - 11
- Knight - 12
- Queen - 13
- King - 14

At the beginning of each session, separate the minor and major arcana into the two separate decks and shuffle each. Place the major arcana deck near the GM. Place the minor arcana deck (with the Fool shuffled into it) in a central location where all the players can reach it.

There are two discard piles—one for minor arcana and one for major arcana. As cards are played, place them into the appropriate discard pile. (Occasionally, certain rules will call for you to look at the top card of a discard pile, so it can be important to note this.)

### Whenever the Fool is drawn, both decks are reshuffled at the end of the round.

### No tarot?

One of the reasons *His Majesty* *the Worm* separates the major and minor arcana decks is to compensate for the fact that not everybody who wants to play this game necessarily has a tarot deck lying around. The mechanics can be replicated, in a pinch, by using a twenty-sided die (a d20) as a stand-in for the GM’s deck and a standard deck of playing cards (with one joker to represent the Fool) for the players. The numbers will be a little different, but the logic and game balance will be the same.

### Random number generation

You can replicate the randomization of polyhedral dice with tarot cards if you so wish.

- The major arcana can act as a d20 (if you redraw when you get the World [XXI]).
- The minor arcana suits can replicate a d4.
- The minor arcana is essentially a d14.
- Dividing the minor arcana in half gives you a weird d7. This can act as a d6 if you redraw on the queen and king.

And, lastly, one of the most random and evocative types of generation you can get from the tarot is *inspiration*. If you’re familiar with the “meanings” of the tarot, you can use those meanings to inform the environments, characters, and events of your game. If you’re not familiar with the traditional tarot interpretation, you can just look at the cool art and feel inspired.

title: Tests of Fate
body:
When an adventurer’s action within the game's narrative is uncertain, the GM calls for a **test of fate**.

Adventurers have four **attributes**, rated 1-4. Each represents an “approach” towards problem solving, and says a lot about *how* an adventurer achieves their goal.

The GM determines which attribute is most relevant to the test’s outcome. To do this, they ask questions of the player to find out how, exactly, they are attempting the action. The player's description will inform which attribute is being tested.

### Attributes

Swords: Swords represents strength and skill with weapons. Test Swords to bend the bars of your cell or tip over a heavy bookshelf onto an unsuspecting goblin.

Pentacles: Pentacles represents swiftness and slyness. Test Pentacles to sneak past a deathknight or slip the sea witch’s conch into your bag without her noticing.

Cups: Cups represents wisdom and training. Test Cups to activate an ancient clockwork mechanism or coax a wild winter wolf to accept a gift of meat from your hand.

Wands: Wands represents willpower and charisma. Test Wands to convince an art critic that your petrified companion is actually avant-garde art or overcome the dominating gaze of a vampire.

If the player describes being sneaky or quick, the GM will call for a test of Pentacles; if the player describes being mystical or eloquent, the GM will call for a test of Wands—and so forth.

To test fate, the player draws a minor arcana card and adds the associated attribute to the value of the card.

### Example

- You test Pentacles and draw a IV of Pentacles. Your adventurer’s Pentacles score is a 2. Your total value is 6.

- You test Pentacles and draw a Knight of Wands. Your adventurer’s Pentacles score is 2 and a Knight has a value of 12. Your total value is 14.

There are four possible outcomes to a test of fate.

### Success

If the total value is 14+, the result is a success. The GM describes how the adventurer succeeds in their stated goal.

### Failure

If the total value is 13 or less, the result is a failure. The GM describes how the adventurer fails and asks what they want to do next.

### Great success

If the total value is 14+ *and* the player drew the suit being tested on the initial draw (not from pushing fate or another source), the result is a great success. Not only does the adventurer succeed, but they succeed extremely well, going above and beyond what was expected.

The GM should invite the player to embellish how *impressive*, how *effortless*, how *quick*, or how *thorough* their success was.

### Great failure

If the player pushes fate *and* the total value is still 13 or less, the test is a great failure. The GM describes a *new* significant setback, bad situation, or harmful repercussion as a result. See “Pushing Fate.”

Additional advice for the GM on adjudicating tests of fate can be found under The blessing of chaos.

### Challenge Actions

The Challenge Phase is a subsystem for handling dangerous situations blow-by-blow. Challenge Actions have occasional similarities to the test of fate rules—for example, favor and disfavor can adjust a Challenge Action’s total value. However, there are many important differences: for example, Challenge Actions are not bound by fate and you cannot push fate on Challenge cards. For the specific rules on how the Challenge Phase handles actions, see Challenge Actions.

title: Pushing fate
body:
If the result of the test is a failure, the player may opt to **push fate**. Pull an additional card and add its value to the original total. If the total result of the two cards plus the attribute is 14+, the test succeeds as normal. You can never achieve a great success if you push fate. If the total result is 13 or less, the test becomes a great failure.

When you push fate and achieve a great failure, you not only fail to achieve what you set out to do, you make things even worse.

Narratively, a great failure creates new obstacles to overcome or severely hampers the adventurers’ path forward. For example, if a thief achieves a great failure while picking a lock, the sound of the broken lockpick jammed in the door alerts a passing guard, who catches the thief red-handed. Or, if a templar suffers a great failure when attempting to intimidate the ogre, the ogre flies into a rage and sucker-punches the templar in a surprise attack.

Additionally, a great failure inflicts a mechanical penalty on the adventurer who failed. If the situation is a dangerous situation, the GM can inflict a Wound on the adventurer. If the situation isn’t life threatening to begin with, an effect—representing frustration, sorrow, madness, exertion, or some other emotional state—might be more appropriate. For example, the GM might say that until the adventurer’s next encampment they become Exhausted (suffering the Exhaust effect) because they have overexerted themselves.

### Pushing fate with the Fool

The Fool has a value of 0.

- If you pull the Fool initially during a test of fate, you can push fate as normal. This could turn the test from a failure to a success or to a great failure.
- If you pull the Fool when pushing fate, your result automatically becomes a great failure.

When the Fool is drawn, remember to shuffle both the minor and major arcana decks.

title: Example test of fate
body:
**GM:** The black dragon seems to be asleep. A rattling snore issues from its nose, as if it’s congested. Its eyes are closed, and occasionally it licks its lips with a long, forked tongue.

**Phynn:** And you said that my cup is under it?

**GM:** Yeah, like, not right under it—but on its bed of gold, which is all spread out around the dragon. So it’s near it. You can reach the cup if you’re careful.

**Phynn:** OK, I want to sneak up to the bed of gold and steal my ancestral cup.

**GM:** OK, that will be a test of fate. Test Pentacles.

*Phynn draws from the minor arcana deck and gets an 8 of* *Swords. He realizes that the odds are good since he needs a* *total of 14.*

**Phynn:** That’s an 8 of Swords plus my Pentacles score of 2. That’s a 10 total. I’m gonna push fate.

*Phynn draws again and gets a 10 of Wands.*

**Phynn:** Awesome. That’s 20 total. That’s a success.

**GM:** Awesome. You sneak closer and closer to the dragon. At one point, the snoring stops and becomes a choking cough. A little cloud of acid fog smokes out of the dragon’s nostrils, but then the snoring begins again. You reach out and grab your cup. Now you have your ancestral cup in your hands, and you’re still sitting in a room with a sleeping dragon. What do you do now?

title: Favor and disfavor
body:
Sometimes circumstances can influence a test of fate positively or negatively.

When beneficial factors would aid an adventurer, they are said to have **favor**. Favor grants +3 to the total value in a test of fate.

When negative factors would hinder an adventurer, they have **disfavor**. Disfavor subtracts –3 from the total value in a test of fate.

Favor and disfavor are not cumulative. You do not apply additional adjustments for having multiple helpful or hindering factors. For example, if you have several favorable factors, just note that you have favor and add +3.

Favor and disfavor cancel each other out. If there are both helpful and hindering factors, you simply make the test of fate as normal. Because favor and disfavor are not cumulative, you do not consider how many factors weigh on either side; multiple favorable factors may be canceled out by one disfavor factor.

### Relevant motifs

If one of your motifs is meaningfully related to the test of fate, you gain favor on the test of fate. See Motifs for more information.

### Resolve

Resolve represents an adventurer’s fortitude as they pursue their quests—fortitude that dwindles as you go deeper and deeper into the Underworld. You may elect to spend a point of Resolve *prior* to a test of fate in order to gain favor on that test. See Resolve for more information.

### Aiding others

It is usually assumed that adventurers fill various niches and take on different roles during the Crawl. One is the scout and always does the reconnaissance, another is typically the watchman for the group, and another always forages for herbs. In these cases, the adventurer most suited for the task simply makes the test of fate. Sometimes, however, players will have the opportunity to work together on a test of fate.

If two players can collaborate meaningfully, the acting player gets favor (+3) on the test of fate.

Adding more people to the mix isn’t necessarily helpful. It’s usually best to let the best-suited adventurer take point and have aid provided by the person most interested in helping.

The caveat about aiding another is that both participating adventurers are affected by the consequences of the test. If the test of fate is successful, both succeed. If the test fails, both adventurers fail. However, it’s important to note that the player who takes the lead and actually draws gets to determine whether or not they push fate. In the case of great failures, both adventurers are affected equally.

### Example test of fate with favor

**Dorian:** Alright, I’m going to try and pick the lock on the door with the crank on it.

**GM:** Sure. You have lockpicks right? Go ahead and test fate with Pentacles.

**Chirm:** Can I try and help?

**GM:** How would you help?

**Chirm:** Uh, like, standing beside Dorian and watching what he does and giving him advice.

**GM:** Usually lockpicking is sort of a solo activity just because of, like, space considerations. Do you have a motif that would justify giving advice?

**Chirm:** I mean, she is a “Wealthy Artificer.”

**GM:** Sure, as an artificer, I can see her knowing a lot about locks and mechanisms. Dorian, take favor.

*Dorian’s player draws and gets an Ace of Wands.*

**Dorian:** Oh no. I got a 1. OK, even with favor and my Pentacles score, that’s only a 7 total. Do we want to push?

**Chirm:** I don’t know. I don’t really want to risk it.

**Dorian:** Me neither.

**GM:** OK. So even with Chirm’s advice, Dorian, the door’s lock seems really inscrutable. The two of you can’t figure it out. If you can’t pick the lock, what are you all going to do?

title: Bound by fate
body:
Whether you succeed or fail, your results are bound by fate. You cannot retry the same test unless the circumstances significantly change. If you fail to pick a lock, that lock is beyond your adventurer’s abilities. If you fail to climb a wall, that wall is unclimbable.

But maybe the warrior in the company can bash down the door. And maybe the sorcerer has a magical cloak that allows you to fly over the wall. You’ll have to find another way past an obstacle if you fail in the test.

You can also attempt a test again if the circumstances significantly change. Significant change usually means new ideas, new tools, or a new twist on an old situation.

Because *His Majesty the Worm* is a fundamentally collaborative game, fellow guild members are also bound by fate. If one person attempts something and fails, it’s established that it cannot feasibly be done at present. No fair having each guild member try successively until somebody succeeds. However, additional guild members can attempt alternate methods to bypass the obstacle.

It’s important to note the GM is also bound by fate. The GM may not call for multiple frivolous tests to see if an adventurer can accomplish a single task. The more times a successful test is reattempted, the more chances the player has to fail. The GM may only call for repeated tests when the situation meaningfully changes.

title: Group tests
body:
In the face of discrete challenges, it’s best to have one adventurer be bold and test fate. There are times, however, when the entire guild must test their fates together. For example, the entire guild must sneak into the Tower Gnostic to steal an artifact or must perform the Operetta d’Serpentis perfectly for the master of the Broken Smiles Opera House. In such cases, the GM calls for a group test.

Group tests are accomplished by having two adventurers test fate: the one most qualified and the one least qualified. If there are apparent ties, talk it out to determine who should make the tests.

- If one of the adventurers succeeds in a test of fate, they give **1 hit** to the group test. If they get a great success, they give **2 hits**.
- If one of the adventurers fails in a test of fate, they give **no hits** to the group test. If they suffer a great failure, they subtract **-1 hit**.

The GM totals the amount of hits to determine the success of the group test.

- **2 hits:** Success for the entire group.
- **1 hit:** The group comes short of succeeding and are put in a tight spot.
- **0 hits:** Failure for the entire group.
- **<0 hits:** Disaster for the entire group.

Like other tests of fate, group tests are bound by fate.

### Example group test

**GM:** OK, so what I’m hearing is that you’re all going to try and hold the door closed as the peryton slams into it. I think that’s a group test. Can I get the highest and lowest Swords people to draw?

**Dorian:** I’m a 3 Swords.

**Chirm:** I’m 2.

**GM:** OK, that’s you, Phynn and Chirm.

*Chirm’s player draws from the minor arcana deck and gets a* *IX of Pentacles. Adding her Swords* *2, that’s a total of 11.* *Chirm pushes fate and gets a IV of Wands. That’s a total of* *15. A success.*

**Chirm:** OK, I got a 15 total. That succeeds.

*Phynn’s player draws a V of Swords from the minor arcana* *deck. With his Swords 4, that’s a total of 9. He also pushes* *fate and draws again, drawing a III of Swords. Despite* *having the higher Swords score, he only gets a 12 total. That’s* *a critical failure.*

**Phynn:** Jesus Christ. I thought I had it. But no, critical fail.

**GM:** OK, that critical failure will reduce the success that Chirm generated, so you get 0 hits. The door buckles under the conflict between you and the peryton. Shards of wood and bits of the iron hinges shriek as they break. Phynn, take a Wound as the peryton gores you with its horns. You’re staring it in its weird, blank eyes. What do you guys do?

title: Effects
body:
Terms that describe consequences that happen to characters or objects things like Blind, Destroy, and Heal are called Effects. Each effect has its own rules and implications, explained in the list below.

### Blind

Blinded creatures cannot see or gain any visual information.

- Blinded creatures make all tests and Challenge Actions with disfavor.
- Blinded creatures can’t make missile attacks at all.
- All harmful actions against Blind creatures have favor.

### Control

Controlled creatures obey the order given to them. As soon as the order is completed, or if it cannot be completed, the effect ends.

- During Challenges, Controlled creatures immediately perform the commanded action. The total value for the Controlled action is equal to the value of the action used to Control it.

### Curse

Curse is a generic term for “bad thing” as determined by the GM. Turned to stone by a medusa? Fused with a party member? Changed into a baby? These are all Curses. The GM will tell you what it means.

### Deafen

Deafened creatures cannot hear or gain any auditory information. Speak Incantation is made with disfavor.

### Destroy

Destroyed objects are broken and unusable.

### Disarm

Disarmed creatures drop one held item of their choice.

- A dropped item requires a Recover action to retrieve during Challenges.
- If an adventurer is carrying neither a melee weapon or shield, all attacks against them gain favor.

### Displace

Displaced creatures are moved to another zone, as determined by the initiating creature or effect.

### Exhaust

Exhausted creatures make all tests and Challenge Actions with disfavor.

### Heal

Healed creatures instantly remove one Wound from a condition.

### Inspire

Inspired creatures must immediately role-play one of the seven Dispositions to the best of their ability, following the basic guidelines. The Dispositions are: anger, distaste, sadness, joy, surprise, trust, fear.

### Grow/Shrink

Grown creatures and objects double their original height. Shrunk creatures and objects half their original height.

Gain favor when this would be advantageous (squeezing into holes, sneaking around) and disfavor when it would be disadvantageous (contests of strength).

### Knockout

Knocked-out creatures are unconscious and incapacitated. They cannot take any actions.

### Notch

When an item suffers an attack that compromises its durability, it is Notched. After suffering a certain number of Notches, the item is Destroyed.

- Fragile items are Destroyed after one Notch.
- Items intended for durability are Destroyed after two Notches.
- Items made of tempered steel are Destroyed after three Notches.
- Notched items can be repaired with a tinker's kit or in the City.

### Root

Rooted creatures cannot move from the spot on which they are standing.

- They cannot Avoid, Dash, Dodge, or Move.
- Anybody engaged with a Rooted creature immediately disengages.

### Shroud

Shrouded creatures are invisible. Shrouded creatures are impossible to see without the aid of magic or special senses.

- Typically, if a Shrouded creature stands still and stays quiet, they cannot be deliberately targeted by creatures who can’t see them.
- However, if the Shrouded creature is moving and interacting with their environment, they can be targeted, though all such attempts are made with disfavor.
- Shrouded creatures make harmful actions with favor against creatures who can’t see them.

### Silence

Silenced creatures cannot make any vocal sounds. As such, they cannot cast spells because they cannot Speak Incantations.

### Stun

When Stunned, immediately choose and discard a Challenge card from your hand.

You do not need to Recover from being Stunned. It is an instantaneous effect.

### Trip

Tripped creatures fall prone.

- Prone creatures cannot Avoid, Move, or Dash.
- Melee attacks against prone targets have favor.
- Missile attacks against prone targets have disfavor.
- Anybody engaged with a Tripped creature immediately disengages.

### Not just for Challenges

Many effects have important ramifications during Challenges. However, effects are not “combat only” rules. For example, outside of a Challenge, a trap with the Displace effect can knock an adventurer into a spiked pit. If that adventurer survives, a sorcerer can cast Gust of Wind to give the Displace effect and pull them back out. The GM adjudicates how effects resolve during the normal flow of the game.

The GM and the players interpret the flavor of how effects interact with the world. For example, a dart envenomed with sleeping poison and a blow to the back of the head might both Knockout the target—however, shaking the sleeping person might be enough to wake them up, whereas the person hit in the head would need medical care.

### Effect names

Note that capitalized effect names change conjugation depending on how they're used in game text, but all mean the same thing. For example, a Blinding attack Blinds a creature, after which they are Blinded.

title: The Adventurer
body:
*“He is a prince of the other world on his travels through this one.. The sun, which shines behind him, knows whence he came, whither he is going, and how he will return by another path after many days. He is the spirit in search of experience.”*

*– The Pictorial Key to the Tarot, A. E. Waite*

There are four social classes in the City. The nobles field knights and have the wealth to supply

them with the finest arms and armor. The nobles are the landowners; they make war when it is necessary to defend or expand the City.

The clergy provide for the spiritual needs of the populace and tally the offerings to the many faces of the Monad. The clergy are the learned class; they perform the tasks of chronicling and remembering the histories of the City.

The tradesmen power the economy of the City. This class of skilled workers is not given the privileges or powers of the nobility but they make enough money to avoid the life of the peasants.

The peasants are indentured servants who work for the right to live on the lands of the nobility. They believe strange things.

Adventurers, who delve into the Underworld for treasures and glory, break this system. Despite the halfcentury since the Underworld's appearance, the City still isn't used to this uncomfortably new fifth class.

In many ways, adventurers are lower than peasants, for they do not have legal rights in the City. However, many become richer than even the nobility, for the Underworld boasts fabulous wealth. At once, adventurers are both respected and despised.

title: The Player’s Manifesto
body:
An RPG is simply an exchange of questions and answers between the players and the GM. These questions and answers can have nuance and texture. When playing *His Majesty the Worm*, this manifesto will help you frame your conversations with your GM.

### Be careful, be fierce

You don’t start out a hero. The only thing between you and a salivating dragon’s jaws are a few conditions unchecked on your adventurer sheet. You should never expect the world around you to be fair. You’re not in a tutorial level; your adventurer is journeying through a mythic Underworld that wants them to stay forever and ever. Keeping them alive requires caution and thoughtfulness.

Encountering a dragon is different when your adventurer is inexperienced versus when they’re experienced. At first, the focus might be stealth—how much gold can you get away with before the dragon notices you? After you’ve built up your strength, you might feel confident enough to engage in combat with the dragon. But don’t fight fair. Make sure you choose the battleground. Ambush the dragon. Drop a rock on its head.

And when the going gets tough, don’t be afraid to cut your losses and run away.

### Solve problems orthogonally

You should be trying to make your GM say: “I didn’t even think of that.”

In an RPG, you can do anything. That’s the appeal! When you’re playing a computer game, you can only do the things the game designer programmed in. They anticipated you moving left, right, and down. Going up is out of the question. Not so in a tabletop game.

Most problems aren’t solved by fighting them. People can be reasoned with. Monsters can be placated. Traps can be avoided. Monsters can be led into traps. People can be sold the monster’s guts.

Don’t expect to “use” your talents and motifs to solve a problem. The abilities and items you have listed are just tools—and they’re only one of the many tools in your arsenal. Think outside of your adventurer sheet.

### Engage the world

You don’t have to talk in a silly voice or wear a costume*. You do, however, have to interact with the fiction of the world in a logical way.

The essential way you have to interact with the fictional world is to ask questions. By engaging your GM in a give-and-take, you make the game real. The game world is layered. By asking questions, you begin to understand its bounds.

There are no abilities on your adventurer sheet that give you the sort of insight that asking questions will provide. If you’re looking for a trap, pour water on the ground and see if you can find any trap doors. If you’re looking for a secret door, tap on the walls and listen for something hollow.

The game is about you using your real-life thinking brain to solve problems, overcome obstacles, and figure things out. There are no stats or powers that are going to help you solve the essential issues.

* You can though. We won’t stop you.

### Engage each other

The most essential stats on your adventurer sheet aren't your talents or motifs. The most essential stats are your Bonds with your guild-mates.

The economy of charging Bonds during the Crawl and spending them during the Camp Phase is essential to the flow of *His Majesty the Worm*. As such, make sure you're thinking of ways to engage other players.

- Play to lift other adventurers up. When you see an opportunity for another adventurer to shine, take a step back. Share each other's burdens. Revel in each other's successes.

- Be respectful and considerate. If you want to explore a particular story, engage with your fellow players to make sure they're comfortable with the themes that you're exploring. Don't be “that guy.” Read the goddamn room.

- Let your relationships grow and change. Every session or two, touch base with another player. Discuss how your adventurers feel about each other in light of your most recent experiences. Have rivals become allies? Have allies become best friends? Have best friends become lovers?

- Be funny in character. Be serious in character. Think in character. Stay in character.

### Embrace the chaos

Part of the game is skill. Part of the game is chance. Sometimes, you can’t be careful or fierce enough to avoid a test of fate. And when fate isn’t on your side, you have to embrace it. Having something bad happen doesn’t mean that you’ve made a mistake. It’s just part of the game.

It is easy to create a new adventurer. This is on purpose. If your adventurer dies, throw yourself into the next one. If your adventurer completes their quest, be excited to retire them.

Games without consequences have no teeth. How boring would it be if you knew you would never fail and never die? The essential gimmick of question/answer with the GM would be boring: “How will your adventurer succeed today?” Thus, love the chaos.

*“An incalculable amount of human effort is directed to combating and restricting the nuisance or danger represented by chance.”*

*– Introduction to the I Ching, Carl Jung*

title: Session 0
body:
Sometimes, RPG players are expected to create their characters by themselves and show up on game night expecting to meet everyone else at an inn. This can sometimes lead to problems at the game table. We recommend that the players and the GM get together for a session before play starts to create adventurers and talk about everybody's expectations. This is called “session 0,” and it can go a long way towards making sure everybody is having fun.

### Collaborative game creation

During session 0, the GM should set expectations about what sort of game they will be running. The general assumption with *His Majesty the Worm* is that it will be a megadungeon-based exploration game where the adventurers pursue their own quests. Deviations from this formula should be discussed by the table.

Have a discussion about what everybody enjoys in games:

- Do you have fun with combat? Do you like learning and using the mechanics of the game?

- Do you enjoy intra-party conflict? Does it stress you out?

- Do you enjoy intra-party romance? Does it stress you out?

- Do you enjoy getting deep into your own character's role-playing?

- Do you enjoy spending an evening with your friends?

- Do you enjoy the emerging story told by an RPG?

Lots of players will have opinions about these sources of fun. Some sources will be more interesting to you than others.

Session 0 is also an important opportunity to make sure that sensitive subjects are treated with the respect that they deserve. If the GM plans on including difficult themes in their game, they should make this apparent up front. For example, if you’re intending to deal with themes of slavery in the City, just say so. Role-playing games can be opportunities to confront important realworld issues. They can also be an opportunity to escape these and not think about them at all.

GMs, be respectful when listening to player’s reactions to sensitive subjects. Don’t put players on the spot (e.g., “Are there any triggering subjects that we should avoid?”). Rather, ask open-ended questions that allow for honest feedback. Work together to find out what subjects are and are not appropriate for your friends.

### Collaborative adventurer creation

During session 0, the players go through all steps of the Call to Adventure together. They discuss the sort of characters they want to play. If there are overlaps, players discuss how they feel about them. Maybe the overlaps are interesting (maybe the two dwarf adventurers are related), or maybe one player would prefer to play something that differentiates them.

If a player has questions about a rule’s interpretation, the GM can answer it and the entire table benefits from learning the clarification. If a player wants to ask the GM for a rules change or special permission for something, the GM can run the potential change past the entire table to see if everybody is okay with it. Everybody is kept on the same page.

As the GM hears interesting details about an adventurer’s background, early ages, apprenticeship years, etc., they can jot down plot ideas. Maybe that long lost brother can come back. Maybe they can make that failed marriage important.

The GM can also use this time to smooth over potential difficulties. One of the players wants to play a cannibal. Is that appropriate for this game and this party?

As part of the Call to Adventure, the players announce their adventurers’ initial quests. The GM can veto these quests or suggest changes to make them more interesting.

### Collaborative guild creation

### Restrictions foster creativity

It’s said that necessity is the mother of invention. If that’s true, we would add our own truism: restrictions are the mother of creativity.

It can be hard for (even experienced) players to choose a compelling character or guild concept ex nihilo. A GM who provides some structure to session 0 can plant seeds of creativity for the players.

For example, perhaps the GM runs an underfolk-only game. Or, perhaps they run a game where the guild is the Secret Pope’s Secret Strike Force.

At first blush, these restrictions might be surprising for players. They might wonder how they can distinguish themselves from each other if everybody is of the same kith or path (or both). However, we’ve found that true distinction comes when the players don’t simply play their “race and class.” The more similar characters are on the surface, the less similar they are in truth.

The adventurers begin the game as members of the same guild. During session 0, over the course of the Call to Adventure, the players fill out the guild roster sheet collaboratively;.

As everyone talks about their adventurers, the GM can try and encourage a guild theme. Are the players all pirates? All dedicated templars? All noble ladies? All named Greg?

Collectively decide:

- What is the name of your guild?

- Why are you adventuring together?

- How did you meet?

- Is there a guild leader?

- What are the looting rights?

Role-playing games have been compared to sex. You usually do it with friends. Sometimes you pay someone to be your dungeon master. Sometimes safe words help. Sometimes you don’t need them. Ultimately, it’s important that everybody involved enthusiastically consents to the stuff that’s going on and everybody is having fun.

*“Dark hallways. Windowless rooms. Stairs. Then a new voice: ‘I’m lost. Out of food. Low on water. No sense of direction. Oh God..’.. ‘There’s something here. It’s following me. No, it’s stalking me. I’ve been stalked by it for days but for some reason it’s not attacking. It’s waiting, waiting for something. I don’t know what. Holloway Roberts. Menomonie, Wisconsin. I’m not alone here. I’m not alone.’”*

*– House of Leaves, Mark Z. Danielewski*

title: The Call to Adventure
body:
Creating an adventurer means heeding the call to adventure. When you create an adventurer, you answer questions and make a series of decisions. This will result in a character with a background, a history, equipment, and connections to other adventurers.

Track the choices of the Call to Adventure and subsequent play on your adventurer sheet. A full version of the adventurer sheet can be printed at *hismajestytheworm.games*.

### 1. Origin

Your home, your hearth, and your heart are your adventurer’s biggest influences.

- Choose a kith and kin from chapter 4. Write down your kin talent.

- Your kin talent begins as mastered. A mastered talent can be used without spending XP. See Talents for details about talents.

- Choose a path from chapter 5. Put a 4 in the corresponding attribute.

- Write down all of your path’s talents.

- Choose one of your path talents to be mastered.

- The rest of your path talents are in-training.

- Choose a name from the list on your kith’s page or make one up.

- All adventurers have a maximum of 4 Resolve. Note that you start with a full 4 Resolve.

### 2. Fitting in

Puberty is a hard time. There are so many weird changes, and you have to make decisions about your future career way earlier than you want to.

- Tell a story to the table about something your adventurer struggled with while young. Based on the story, put a 1 in one attribute.

- Choose a motif based on your origin story. This might be related to your parents’ professions or an apprenticeship. See Motifs for details about motifs.

### 3. Failed career

You had a shot at a normal life and you blew it. What was your previous job?

- Tell a story to the table about your failed career. Based on your story, put a 2 in one attribute.

- Choose a motif related to your failed career.

### 4. Querent

Adventure calls to you.

- Tell a story to the table about why you’re willing to brave the Underworld. What is your quest? Note it down.

- If it’s important to your group, choose two languages.

### 5. Full-blown weirdo

You set out to become that dreadful, ugly, and unwelcome thing: an adventurer. Your first foray into the Underworld was…what?

- Tell a story about your first adventure into the Underworld. Based on your story, put a 3 in the last attribute.

- Choose a motif based on this adventure. This is your last motif, so think carefully.

- What does your adventurer look like? Briefly describe them to the rest of the guild.

### 6. Guild bonding

Who is in your guild and why are you traveling together?

- Each player declares a Bond with every other player at the table (Bonds). *Bonds are very important for the meta- economy of the game.*

- Get out the guild roster. Note down the members of the guild.

- Collectively give your guild a name and have someone draw the guild’s sigil.

- Collectively determine your looting rights in the terms section of the roster.

- Each player chooses their marching order (first, second, third, etc.) and guild role.

More information about guilds, marching order, and so on, is covered in chapter 3.

### 7. Treats from Ma

Look at the Omphalic Market.

- Choose 1 luxurious item, 5 common items, and as many impoverished items as you want. Keep choosing items until your belt and your backpack are full.

- If any of your talents require specific items (an archwood wand, a bow, heavy armor, poultices, hermetic bottles, etc.), these items count as impoverished items for you during the Call to Adventure. You can have as many as you want.

### Putting it all together

In summation, your adventurer has:

- Attributes set at 4, 3, 2, and 1

- A path

- 1 mastered path talent, 1 mastered kin talent, and 6 path talents in training

- A quest

- 3 motifs

- 4 Resolve

- A full backpack and belt containing 1 luxurious item, 5 common items, and as many impoverished items and items used by your talents as you want

- Bonds with the rest of the guild

- An appearance

- A name

You’re now ready to heed the call to adventure and delve into the Underworld.

### The adventurer sheet

Each section of the adventurer sheet is described in detail on the following pages!

*“Tell me a story. Make it a story of great distances, and starlight. The name of the story will be Time, But you must not pronounce its name. Tell me a story of deep delight.”*

*– “Tell Me a Story,” Robert Penn Warren*

title: Name, kith, and kin
body:
### Knaves, rogues, and scoundrels

Playing murder hobos gets so old so fast. Whee, you killed the barkeep because he looked at you wrong. Whee, you set the tavern on fire.

*His Majesty the Worm* is a game for heroes. You can be dirty, rotten thieves—but at least you have a heart of gold.

Adventurers have a kith and a kin. An adventurer’s kith is their “race”—whether they are human or fay or underfolk or otherwise. In game terms, kith is the broad cultural context that separates them from the rest of the world.

Kin defines an adventurer’s clan, realm, or kingdom, and differentiates that adventurer from others of their kith. Two adventurers with the same kin are from the same sub-group—or maybe even related by blood.

Chapter 4 details the various kith and kin that you can choose from during the Call to Adventure, and provides some sample names.

- You automatically begin with a mastered talent determined by your kin.

- Your kith determines your arête triggers. When all three triggers are checked, you automatically learn your kin’s arête talent.

The kiths and kin are:

### Humans

- Divided into myriad houses

### Fay

- High elves
- Wood elves
- Dark elves
- Gnomes

### Underfolk

- Dwarves
- Halflings
- Trolls

### Orcs

- Earthblooded
- Fireblooded
- Seablooded
- Stormblooded

title: Attributes
body:
### Attributes as class

You might think of each attribute as a rating in one of four jobs: warrior, rogue, scholar, and sorcerer. When a particular task would fall within the purview of one of these jobs, you test fate with that particular attribute.

An adventurer’s abilities are measured by four attributes. The attributes are:

### Swords
Swords is the attribute of warriors. Swords encompasses strength and endurance. It represents bravery, fortitude, directness, forcefulness, and all facets of combat.

### Cups

Cups is the attribute of scholars. Cups encompasses wisdom and learning. It represents cleverness, carefulness, patience, and everything related to the use of tools.

### Pentacles
Pentacles is the attribute of rogues. Pentacles encompasses swiftness and slyness. It represents quickness, quietness, manipulation, and everything related to stealth.

### Wands

Pentacles is the attribute of rogues. Pentacles encompasses swiftness and slyness. It represents quickness, quietness, manipulation, and everything related to stealth.

Wands is the attribute of sorcerers. Wands encompasses your willpower and mysticism. It represents persuasiveness, showmanship, spirit, passion, and everything related to the occult.

Adventurers have a spread of attributes ranked 4, 3, 2, and 1. Your highest attribute (4) will be the same as the path you belong to (Chapter 5: The Four Paths).

title: Quests
body:
Every adventurer has a reason to go down into the Underworld. This is called your quest.

Your quest is your adventurer’s motivating objective. It is *discrete* and *achievable*.

So, “Find the Grail of Mythrys” is a good quest, but “Get rich” is a bad quest. Yes, the Grail of Mythrys will make you rich, but riches is not what you're questing for.

### Example quests

- Capture a cockatrice and haul it back to the City alive so that the Order of Alchemists can save your petrified brother.

- Kill the vampire who turned you into a thrall so that you can be restored to humanity.

- Find the Well of Lethe so that you can forget the terrible things you’ve done and have a chance at a happy life.

- Get a trophy from a dragon so that you can impress the pirate crew that mutinied against you.

- Pluck a nega-rose from the Grave of the First Dead so that the Witchmother accepts your proposal of marriage to her daughter.

Players and the GM should talk over their quests during session 0. The GM should set expectations for what’s reasonable to quest for. The players should talk about adventures that would be interesting to them.

It’s the GM’s job to place each player’s quest objectives into the Underworld and hedge them with interesting, open-ended challenges. They should pepper hints, rumors, and associated characters into the game world so that players have things to explore and paths towards victory. See Create a path to success for more information about how the GM does this.

Like rumors that you hear in the City, what you hear about your quest may or may not be correct. There might be twists. There might be competition. There might be trouble.

title: Motifs
body:
You play an adventurer—a homeless mercenary who voluntarily delves into the depths of a mythical dungeon in hopes of treasure and glory and gods only know what else. But every adventurer in the Underworld has lived another life. Your motifs speak to the life that you lived before you became an adventurer.

A motif is a short phrase that defines a moment in your adventurer’s history. Motifs have two primary uses:

- When your adventurer has a motif that would prepare them or make them particularly qualified for a test of fate, you have favor on that test (+3 to the total).

- You can bid lore to ask the GM questions about a subject if you have a motif that is appropriate to the question you’re asking; see Lore,.

A motif is made up of two parts: a descriptor and the name of a profession. To create a motif, combine two words from the lists on the following page, or create your own. An adventurer only ever has three motifs.

You should never feel locked into the choices you make about your adventurer. You may change a motif during the City Phase if you and the GM feel it’s appropriate.

*“We’ve met before.” “Right! When I was a pirate’s ship-boy.” “And I was a wizard’s apprentice.”*

*– Ill Met in Lankhmar, Fritz Leiber*

title: Bonds
body:
The relationships you have with all the other members of your guild are called Bonds. Bonds are reflected on your adventurer sheet in terms of simple sentences: “I am Petyr’s mentor,” or “Grendel is my ally.” Your Bonds become charged when you *play them to the hilt* or when they *put you in danger*.

If you play a Bond to the hilt, you exemplify the relationship represented by the Bond. Basic suggestions for this role-play are given in the descriptions of the example Bonds below; however, the GM can call for the Bond to be charged by other examples of excellent roleplaying, too.

- Players, just ask the GM when you think you’ve done a great job. GMs, be generous and honest.

If your Bond puts you in danger, you make a choice that puts your adventurer at a disadvantage or takes a big risk for the sake of exemplifying their Bond.

- Players, ask your GM if you think your choice really jeopardizes you. GMs, be generous and honest.

Charges may be burned during the Camp Phase to heal Wounds and recover Resolve. **For each charge you burn,**

**you heal 1 Wound or regain 1 Resolve.** See Recovery for full details.

By way of example, the Bonds below are illustrated using characters from *Firefly* and The Lord of the Rings. We figured this was geek lingua franca.

### Ally

Your allies are guild-mates that you are professional and amiable with. This is the default Bond.

**Examples:** Wash and Kaylee, Aragorn and Gandalf

- Charge this Bond when you make your ally laugh both in and out of character.

### Adversary

If you have a significant problem with a guild-mate, you’re probably their adversary. This isn’t an excuse to be an ass to another player, but it’s an opportunity for interesting and fair conflict.

**Examples:** Mal and Jayne, Boromir and Aragorn

- Charge this Bond when you witness your adversary fail a test of fate.

### Big/Little

There's a special relationship between a diminutive halfling and her huge troll “brother.” If one adventurer is bigger than the other and you use this to your advantage, this is the Bond for you.

Example: Éowyn and Merry

- You both charge this Bond when your big/little aids you in a test of fate with your weakest attribute.

### Best Friend

You wouldn't let your best friend go on an adventure without you. You're there for each other, thick or thin.

**Examples:** Mal and Zoe, Merry and Pippin

- You both charge this Bond when you reveal a secret to your best friend.

### Love

If both players are cool with it, use this Bond to represent someone you are in a romantic relationship with. If the relationship is one-sided, use the Unrequited Love Bond.

**Examples:** Zoe and Wash, Faramir and Éowyn

- Charge this Bond when you do something gushy and romantic for your partner, whether it’s writing an in-character love sonnet or risking your neck to pick a bunch of flowers for them.

### Master/Henchman

Players can be hirelings. When you have a managerial vs. subservient relationship with another guild-mate, this is your Bond.

**Examples:** Mal and Wash, Frodo and Sam

- Masters charge this Bond when they give their henchman an agreed-upon payment or compensation.

- Henchmen charge this Bond when they use one of their Camp Actions to benefit their master but not themselves.

### Mentor/Mentee

Whether a parent, parent-figure, or merely the guild leader, a mentor guides and shapes the life of a mentee.

**Examples:** Shepherd Book and River, Gandalf and Frodo

- Mentees charge this Bond when they ask the mentor for advice and it is given.

- Mentors charge this Bond when a mentee follows their advice.

### Rival

You are in competition with your rival. You might want the same woman, the most kills, or something weirder.

Example: Legolas and Gimli

- Charge this Bond when you witness your rival succeed on a test of fate.

### Sibling

Your first adventures were raiding your mother's cookie jar together. Now, you're guild-mates.

**Examples:** Simon and River, Boromir and Faramir

- Charge this Bond when you provide aid to your sibling in a test of fate.

### Unrequited Love

He’s just not that into you. If both players are cool with it, use this Bond to represent how you feel about a would-be suitor or ex-lover.

**Examples:** Simon and Kaylee, Aragorn and Éowyn

- Charge this Bond when you do something kind for your love and they rebuff you or turn you down.

### Ward

You have a guild-mate that you look out for. It’s important they survive.

Example: Frodo, River

- When your Ward survives an entire Challenge without taking a Wound, charge this Bond.

### Negative bonds and “That Guy”

OK, let’s talk real quick about the connotation of some of these negative Bonds and problem players.

Some of these Bonds (Unrequited Love, Adversary, Rival) seem like they’d incite a bad time with “that guy.” We hope this isn’t true for you. Whenever somebody is being “that guy,” there’s one real solution: talk to them. Maybe you got off track. Maybe there was a miscommunication. Maybe this player has had different experiences and expectations with gaming than the rest of the table. These things can often be worked through.

Moreover, the session 0 rules we’ve included are designed to help mitigate having these experiences in the first place. But, if and when they arise, a frank, adult discussion can serve you well.

The fact of the matter is that some Bonds are, in fact, representative of “negative” relationships and derived from adversarial relationships in the inspirational fiction. We think these can be fun—but only if done with the consent of all parties involved. Table consensus is a prime tool for everybody having a fun time. If the idea of Unrequited Love appeals to you, talk to the table. See who would be interested in that Bond, and make sure the GM is interested in that sort of story.

GMs, talk to your players when they bring these things up. Facilitate communication. Are the players interested in ever moving the Unrequited Love towards Love?

At the end of the day, it’s important that everybody is having fun with the Bonds. If they’re not, just swap them to “Ally.” It’s the default one.

title: Arête
body:
Each adventurer has the capacity to exemplify the platonic ideal of their kin, which is called their arête.

Arête (AIR-uh-tay) is a word of Greek origin meaning virtue, gnosis, excellence, and evolution.

Each kin has an arête talent. Unlike talents associated with an adventurer’s path, arête talents cannot be trained with experience points.

You gain arête when you perform certain accomplishments dependent on your kith. The first time you accomplish each particular deed, put a check mark beside it. When you have checked off all three of your arête triggers, you gain your arête talent. See chapter 4 for a list of your kith’s arête triggers and arête talent.

title: Languages
body:
There are five languages spoken commonly in the City, and a hundred uncommon ones. At a minimum, each adventurer is at least bilingual—choose two languages from the lists below. If you want to learn more languages later, train the Loremaster talent until you’re a skilled linguist.

Alternatively, if tracking languages in your game doesn’t feel fun, don’t do it.

### Vulgaris

Vulgaris, the common tongue, is a creole language, developed from a pidgin mash of Ancient Mannish, Vetus, and Tylwyth. Despite a few decades of official censure by the Cult of Mythrys and the City’s rulership as a “base” tongue, Vulgaris is by far the most common language spoken throughout the Wide World by humans, underfolk, and orcs. Most inhabitants of the City speak it decently well.

### Cant

Cant is the language of the lowborn. It is especially famous as the language of thieves, scoundrels, rogues, and ne’er-do-wells. The language is lilting and filled with rhyming couplets, so that it is quite musical when spoken. It is also filled with seeming banalities, so those who speak the Cant seem to be speaking about nothing at all. For example, two thieves might be discussing a planned heist, but seemingly referring to famous actors, the weather, and breeds of puppies.

Cant is derived from Vulgaris and shares much of its grammar and vocabulary. However, those without proficiency in this language can absolutely not understand a single sentence of it.

### Chivalric

Chivalric is the language of the nobility. All legal and courtly proceedings are conducted in this tongue. If a poor commoner is caught in the justice system without knowledge of this language, the case continues with or without their comprehension.

Chivalric shares much of its grammar and vocabulary with Vulgaris, but is couched in romantic, philosophical, and pseudo-religious argot so that it is absolutely impenetrable by those unlearned in its application.

### Tylwyth

Tylwyth is the ancestral language of the fay and other spirits. Since the fay have dwelt within the bounds of the Wide World for much longer than Mankind, many of the spirits and minor divinities that live there speak Tylwyth almost exclusively.

The fay, as a whole, are known for their love of languages and Tylwyth enjoys a certain fame among scholars and linguists as being a logical, subtle, and beautiful tongue. Careful cultivation by immortal linguists has developed Tylwyth into a purposeful and useful language, like a carefully pruned tree.

### Vetus

Vetus has enjoyed over five-hundred years of consistent use and is the official language of the Cult of Mythrys. As the Cult is the center of academia, almost every written text or scholarly book is written in this language. Scholars would be wise to master it.

Mythrys made the language sacred by declaring that, in order to more deeply understand the Mysteries that he revealed, all adherents of the faith must learn Vetus, and so avoid the pitfalls and stumbling blocks that come with clumsy translation. Those adherents who do not speak it merely go through the motions during religious festivals.

Vetus is written in a flowing cursive script from right to left. It is usually written in an abjad form. The Vetus script is the only language written in the City. Sometimes its script system is (crudely) borrowed for other languages, but books, scrolls, documents, proclamations, and other important texts are only rendered in Vetus.

### Ancient tongues

History has many ancient modes of speech. These are mostly historical footnotes; few texts remain written in these scripts and there are almost no native speakers. However, some scholars study ancient languages to have a deeper connection with their own race, because their obscure branch of study necessitates it, or because of their love of philology.

title: Conditions
body:
The adventurer sheet helps you track your adventurer’s status. Journeying in the Underworld is fraught with peril. It is even rumored that it contains powerful magics that bind your soul to your body. As you journey, you mark conditions to represent the slow degradation of your physical and mental health.

Wounds accumulated during Challenges cause you to mark conditions to represent damage. See Wounds for the grisly details of taking Wounds.

### Stressed

Stressed represents being physically or mentally exhausted.

- Becoming Stressed is usually the result of environmental effects, such as being covered in sewage, being buried alive in a grave, or wading through an icy river.

- Wounds do not cause you to be Stressed.

- You cannot heal any other condition until you are no longer Stressed.

- Learn more about being Stressed.

### Staggered

Staggered represents being off balance and out of breath.

- This condition has no immediate negative effects.

- Staggered is healed automatically during the Camp Phase as long as you’re not Stressed.

- It is usually the first condition players choose when Wounded. It’s kind of a “free hit.”

### Wounded

Your talents can be Wounded. You may have up to two talents Wounded at a time.

- Wounded talents cannot be used until they are healed.

- If you already have two talents Wounded, you must choose another condition to mark.

### Injured

Injured represents being severely hurt.

- If you are Injured, the *next* Wound must give you the Death’s Door condition.

- During the Camp Phase, you must heal the Injured condition before healing Wounded talents.

- Because being Injured puts you in danger of death, most players only take this condition if they have no other choice.

### Death’s Door

Death’s Door represents being (almost) dead. You are unconscious and helpless.

- Because of the nature of the Underworld, if nobody moves to heal you within a watch, you will become undead. See Death’s Door for more details about the nature of Death’s Door.

title: Resolve
body:
You need grit to survive. This is represented with a resource called Resolve. Resolve represents an adventurer’s fortitude as they pursue their quests— fortitude that dwindles as you go deeper and deeper into the Underworld.

You have 4 points of Resolve.

You may use Resolve in the following ways:

- When the GM calls for a test of fate, you may spend a Resolve to gain favor on the test. This can only be done before the test is actually made. Favor allows you to add +3 to the total result of the draw.

- You may spend a Resolve to gain favor on a Challenge Action, adding +3 to the total value.

- Certain talents require the expenditure of Resolve.

You burn charged Bonds to restore your Resolve during the Camp Phase.

title: Lore
body:
Your adventurer’s motifs define what they are knowledgeable about. You may ask the GM a question related to these motifs and expect an honest answer. We call this bidding lore. When you bid lore, you’re essentially asking “Would my adventurer know this?”

Lore represents things that your adventurer knows that you, as the player, might not. This might include the vulnerability of a particular monster, the taboos or habits of a foreign people, or the special properties of a particular plant variety.

You may bid lore 4 times between Camp Phases. Your lore bid uses are reset when you Camp.

When you bid lore, the GM has three potential responses:

- “Yes, you know about this.” The GM then gives a detailed answer. Check off one of your lore bid uses.

- “No, you wouldn’t know about this with that motif.” You don’t check off a lore bid use if you don’t receive an answer.

- “That question doesn’t seem fair game.” The GM then explains why the lore bid question was too broad or vague. You may rephrase or reframe the question.

*“They are wrought of ithildin that mirrors only starlight and moonlight, and sleeps until it is touched by one who speaks words now long forgotten in Middleearth. It is long since I heard them, and I thought deeply before I could recall them to my mind.”*

*– The Fellowship of the Ring, J. R. R. Tolkien*

### Lore bid questions are discrete

You cannot ask, “Have I ever seen anything like this?” The question is too broad.

You may ask, “Do I know what the monsters depicted on the bas-relief are?”

### Lore bid answers are thorough

The GM cannot say, “You’re not sure, but you think they might be related to dragons.” If an answer is this vague, the player does not need to bid lore. GMs should simply tell them this hint.

The GM may say, “You know that these are dragons because you’ve seen their iconography before. As a dragon hunter, though, you recognize that these are fire drakes. These dragons are flightless and live in rivers of lava under the earth. They are famous for their uncontrolled rages and fiery breath.”

### Lore bid questions aren’t a replacement for clever thinking

You cannot ask, “How do you defeat a dragon?” This question is too broad and too subjective.

You may ask, “Do I know if a drake has any special vulnerabilities?”

title: Talents
body:
Talents are the special abilities that set you apart from the rest of the filthy peasants and help you survive delves into the Underworld. A talent can either be unknown, mastered, in training, or mentored.

### Unknown talents

All talents from paths other than your own are unknown. You can, however, train these talents using the mentoring rules below.

Talents from other kith and kin are always unknown. They cannot be trained.

### Mastered talents

You begin play with two mastered talents. When you create your adventurer, select one of your path’s talents to master. Your kin talent is also automatically mastered.

You may use mastered talents at any point as long as they’re not Wounded and you can pay costs associated with them (such as Resolve).

### In-training path talents

All talents from your path that you have not mastered are automatically in training.

You may only use in-training path talents if you spend XP to power them. You must spend 1XP every time you wish to use one of these talents.

Once you have spent 7XP powering an in-training path talent, it becomes mastered.

### Mentored talents from other paths

To train a talent from another path, you must find a willing trainer who has mastered that talent. Both the trainer and the adventurer must use the Train Camp Action or the Train City Action.

During this action, the adventurer in training invests XP into the mentored talent. The adventurer in training may then use the new talent a number of times equal to the XP invested.

Note that this differs from training talents from your own path. You choose to spend XP to power an unmastered path talent on a per-use basis, whereas you invest XP into a cross-path talent during training. You do not need an instructor to mentor talents from your path.

Once you have spent 7XP on training a talent with a mentor, it becomes mastered.

title: Experience
body:
Experience points (XP) represent an adventurer’s skills improving as they adventure. You spend XP to use talents that you have not yet mastered.

During play, if nobody else is currently pursuing their quest, you may declare your quest to the rest of your guild.

- If everybody agrees to help you, every player (including you) gains 3XP.

- When the guild completes a quest, every player gains 3XP.

A guild can only pursue one quest at a time. Once one quest has been completed, someone else should speak up and share the reason they’re descending into the Underworld. If the group agrees to help them, the guild starts the next quest.

Pursuing and fulfilling quests is the *main* way to accumulate experience. There are two other ways to accumulate experience points:

- When your guild fulfills a contract for an employer, everybody in the guild gains 1XP. See Current Contracts for information on contracts.

- When you take the Carousing City Action, you spend your gold to gain experience points (but risk a splitting hangover). See City Actions for details on this City Action.

### Wide, not deep, growth

It’s worth noting that adventurers in *His Majesty the Worm* grow “wide” not “deep.” That is, XP allows you to use and master more talents, broadening the options available to you. You do not gain bigger numbers, +1s, more hit points, etc.

In addition to XP, there are two other types of growth that adventurers benefit from. The first is arête, a feature of your kith. The second is “weirdness.” As you journey through the Underworld, you get weirder. You accumulate scars, mutations, magical items, pets, mutilations, phobias, etc. There are no rules governing the latter. Finding out how your adventurer gets weirder is essentially the whole game.

title: Animal companions and familiars
body:
Adventurers sometimes take pets into the Underworld— hunting falcons, small but vicious dogs, trained dire moths, riding boars, and so on.

As a general rule, you may have as many animal companions travel with your guild as you can carry feed for. Animal companions need to eat each Camp Phase (just as you do). If they do not, they begin to starve. Starving animals might abandon you entirely in search of food.

Animal companions do not have slots for carrying items. You must carry your animal’s feed.

The Beast Master talent can train these animal companions so that they can serve at need during dungeon delves. Trained animals will perform one of their commands at your direction. Most normal animals can only learn three commands.

If necessary, commands might prompt a test of fate. If the animal is uniquely suited to the test (e.g., monkeys are great at climbing and grabbing stuff, horses are great at pulling), the test is made with favor. Otherwise, no bonuses are added to the test of fate.

If nobody in your guild has the Beast Master talent, you may pay animal trainers in the City to train your pets for you (see The Hippodrome of Amet).

### Hirelings?

There are no rules for hirelings, henchmen, mercenaries, etc. because that is what *you* are playing. If you’re going into the Underworld, you’re an *adventurer*. You’re going down there for some reason, not just gold. Nobody can go into the Underworld unless they’re a member of a guild and nobody is special enough to join a guild unless they’re going to be played by a player.

title: War pigs
body:
During Challenges, an animal companion does not act unless its owner uses the Command action to have it perform one of its known commands. The GM interprets the pet’s actions, as even well-trained animals will use their own logic and understanding in stressful situations. An animal companion shares its master’s Initiative.

### Wounds and healing

Unlike adventurers, animal companions usually only have two conditions: Staggered and Injured. Animals do not have talents to Wound. Once an animal companion is Injured, the very next Wound it takes will kill it.

The exception to this rule is if the animal is a familiar: a familiar’s owner may spend a Resolve to reduce a killing blow (see Beast Master,). These familiars are out of the action but not dead.

Animal companions lose the Staggered condition if fed during the Camp Phase.

A player may spend one of their charged Bonds to heal their animal’s Injured condition during step 4 of the Camp Phase. Animals can also benefit from the Heal effect.

title: Pack space and gear
body:
### Filthy lucre

Gold can be easy to get and easy to lose in the adventuring life. Money is used to resupply with essential gear during the City Phase.

There is only one denomination of money accepted in the City: gold coins marked with a pentacle. These coins are found in hidden troves in the Underworld.

Gold coins (abbreviated “g”) take up slots in your belt or your pack. You can stack 100g to a slot.
